name: apple-hig

# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 topic skills, and original article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below. Read that family's `SKILL.md`, then only the
   article references needed for the task. Nested skills are explicitly read by
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
3. For an exact component, technology, or unfamiliar term, search the
   [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md). It links directly to local
   article references. Do not load the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |
| Charts, images, text views, embedded web content | [Content](subskills/apple-hig-content/SKILL.md) |
| Lists, collections, split views, tab views, disclosure and grouping | [Layout and organization](subskills/apple-hig-layout-and-organization/SKILL.md) |
| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |
| Touch, keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controllers and sensors | [Inputs](subskills/apple-hig-inputs/SKILL.md) |
| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Apply the guidance

- **Design:** connect each important choice to the user's task and target
  platform. Include necessary interaction states, adaptation, and accessibility.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

Platform: iOS, standard app mode; no Assistive Access flow is requested. Body text is hard-coded to 12 pt and clips when enlarged to 200%. Unavailable departure times are indicated only with red text, available ones only green. Pay is a custom icon with no accessible name. Removing a traveller requires a three-finger swipe with no onscreen alternative. Booking failures play a sound with no visual or text message. Contrast colors, actual focus order and screenshots are not supplied.

# Apple HIG: Foundations

Start with accessibility, inclusion, and privacy constraints that affect the whole experience. Load the specific visual or interaction foundation for the decision at hand, then its platform subsection. Prefer semantic system components, colors, typography, and materials; test adapted layouts, user settings, and real contexts. Treat numerical specifications as reference facts and preserve their platform and unit distinctions.

# Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Typography Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. ## Contents - [Ensuring legibility](#Ensuring-legibility) - [Conveying hierarchy](#Conveying-hierarchy) - [Using system fonts](#Using-system-fonts) - [Using custom fonts](#Using-custom-fonts) - [Supporting Dynamic Type](#Supporting-Dynamic-Type) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) - [Specifications](#Specifications) - [Resources](#Resources) - [Change log](#Change-log) ## Ensuring legibility Test type at real viewing distances, lighting conditions, and supported devices. Enlarge hard-to-read text, improve foreground/background contrast, or choose a more legible face. Prefer Regular, Medium, Semibold, or Bold over Ultralight/Thin/Light, especially at small sizes. Thin custom faces often need sizes above the recommendations. |Platform|Default|Minimum| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| ## Conveying hierarchy Combine size, weight, and color to distinguish levels, and preserve those relationships as text grows. Limit typeface families so differences retain meaning. Prioritize content people intend to read when scaling: body/dialogue may need growth while tab labels or transient damage numbers need not grow equally. ## Using system fonts San Francisco includes Pro, Compact, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Hebrew, and Mono variants; all listed except Mono also have rounded alternatives. New York is a complementary serif family. Variable fonts interpolate weights and optical design continuously for the exact point size, rather than requiring separate Text/Display font choices except in limited design tools. SF offers widths such as Condensed/Expanded and weights from Ultralight through Black; equivalent SF Symbol weights enable precise matching. Use semantic text styles to express hierarchy through coordinated weight, size, and leading, and to inherit Dynamic Type/accessibility adjustments where supported. Modify symbolic traits for emphasis or line spacing when justified. Loose leading supports long passages or wide columns; tight leading can fit constrained rows, but avoid it for three or more lines. Access system fonts through platform APIs (`default`, `serif`, and the font-design constants), without embedding the files. Runtime tracking adapts by size automatically; mockups may need the tracking values below. ## Using custom fonts Check custom faces against platform size recommendations and actual conditions. Implement Dynamic Type and Bold Text behavior equivalent to the system faces. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can support Dynamic Type in games; if unsuitable, offer a separate text-size adjustment. ## Supporting Dynamic Type Dynamic Type is available in iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS. Test every supported size, including Larger Accessibility Text on iPhone/iPad. Scale meaningful glyphs as well as text; SF Symbols integrate automatically. Preserve useful information at the largest accessibility size rather than aggressively truncating. Give labels enough lines and avoid truncation in scrolling regions unless a detail view exposes the full text. Stack inline timestamps/glyphs beneath or above primary text, grow containers, and reduce columns when width becomes cramped. Keep important content toward the top and the overall hierarchy stable. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS SF Pro is standard; New York is also available. ### macOS SF Pro is standard and New York is available to Mac Catalyst apps. macOS has no Dynamic Type. Match standard-control typography with the relevant NSFont methods: `controlContentFont`, `labelFont`, `menuFont`, `menuBarFont`, `messageFont`, `paletteFont`, `titleBarFont`, `toolTipsFont`, `userFont`, `userFixedPitchFont`, `boldSystemFont`, and `systemFont`, each with its `ofSize:` parameter. ### tvOS SF Pro is standard, with New York also available. ### visionOS SF Pro is standard; specify text styles explicitly when using New York. Body/title Dynamic Type styles are bolder, and Extra Large Title 1/2 support wide editorial compositions. Prefer readable 2D text with little or no extrusion. Test full-scale designs through different viewing scales. Default white text contrasts with glass; test custom colors against diverse surroundings. Without a container background, bold can improve visibility; do not rely on unpredictable cast shadows. Billboard labels associated with 3D objects toward the viewer, normally rotating around the y-axis so the baseline stays perpendicular to the line of sight. ### watchOS SF Compact is standard, New York is available, and complications use SF Compact Rounded. ## Specifications Values below preserve the source’s factual measurements. Sizes, leading, and line heights are in points; tracking is given in thousandths of an em and points. Emphasis can be applied through SwiftUI `bold()` or UIKit `UIFontDescriptor` `traitBold`; the resulting emphasized weight varies by style. item.text: The specification verifies five accessibility problems: unnamed Pay control, gesture-only removal, clipped enlarged text, color-only availability, and sound-only failure feedback. I’ll prioritize them by their effect on completing checkout. Contrast and focus order remain unverified because the specification doesn’t supply them.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > /tmp/hig-eval-_ceysv1c/result.md <<'EOF'
# iPhone trip checkout accessibility audit

This is a specification audit of "'`interface.md`, for iOS in standard app mode. Five findings are verified by explicit statements in that file; their runtime manifestations have not been tested. All five should be corrected before checkout release. Ranking below is an audit decision based on task impact, not an Apple severity classification.

## Prioritized findings and decisions

| Rank | Verified evidence and impact | Correction and source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — P1 | Pay is a custom icon with no accessible name. A screen-reader user cannot reliably identify the action that commits payment; voice targeting is also impaired. | Use a visible **Pay** label and expose a button named “Pay”, with enabled/busy state. Treat any accompanying decorative icon as part of that single control, not a second focus stop. Meaningful descriptions and control labels: [Accessibility — Vision](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Vision), [Mobility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Mobility). |
| 2 — P1 | Removing a traveller requires a three-finger swipe, with no onscreen alternative. Users unable to perform the gesture cannot correct the traveller list. | Add a visible Remove button for each traveller, with a distinct accessible name such as “Remove Alex Morgan”. Use one ordinary activation path across touch and assistive input. Remove the mandatory complex gesture; any retained shortcut is optional and must not conflict with system gestures. [Accessibility — Mobility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Mobility). |
| 3 — P1 | Body text is fixed at 12 pt and clips at 200% enlargement. Enlarged checkout information becomes unreadable. | Use a semantic body style or equivalent preference-driven scaling, with 17 pt at the iOS default setting as the design baseline. Allow wrapping, growing rows and vertical scrolling; stack crowded content. Preserve complete information at 200% and all supported larger accessibility sizes. The verified failure is clipping/scaling, not a claim that 12 pt violates the 11 pt iOS minimum. [Accessibility — Vision](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Vision), [Typography — Supporting Dynamic Type](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography#Supporting-Dynamic-Type). |
| 4 — P1 | Available departures use only green text; unavailable departures use only red. People who cannot distinguish those colors lose the availability information needed to choose a trip. | Add visible “Available” / “Unavailable” text beside each time and include the status in its accessible representation. Color may remain supplementary. Expose selection and enabled state separately; an unavailable time remains readable but cannot be selected for purchase. This selection behavior is a proposed product decision. [Accessibility — Vision](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Vision). |
| 5 — P1 | Booking failures produce sound without a visual or text message. Users who cannot hear the sound receive no stated failure feedback. | Show a persistent, accessible text message identifying failure and the supported next step. Announce it through the accessibility status mechanism; retain it until resolved or explicitly dismissed. Sound and optional haptics supplement the message. Never infer payment or booking status that the backend has not confirmed. [Accessibility — Hearing](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Hearing), [Cognitive](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Cognitive). |

## Worked before/after

The names and times below are illustrative fixtures, not additional observations.

**Before, as specified:** 12 pt body text clips at 200%; 09:30 is green and 10:00 red without status text; the payment icon has no name; Alex can be removed only by a three-finger swipe; a failed booking sounds a tone without a message.

**After, proposed:** the body follows the text-size preference and wraps in growing containers. Departure rows read “09:30 — Available” and “10:00 — Unavailable”. Alex’s row includes a visible Remove button, exposed as “Remove Alex Morgan, button”. Checkout has one visible and accessible “Pay” button. A confirmed unsuccessful booking shows “Booking failed. Review your details and try again” only when retry is known to be safe. A status-unknown response instead shows “We couldn’t confirm your booking. Check booking status before paying again”, with a supported status-check action.

Framework-independent behavior contract:

```text
bodyStyle = semanticBody(userTextPreference, userBoldPreference)
layout = verticallyScrollable, intrinsicRowHeights, wrappingText
when horizontal content no longer fits: stack content in reading order
never shrink body text or clip essential information to retain row height

for each departure:
    show(time, availabilityText)
    expose(time + availabilityText, selectedState, enabledState)
    permit selection only when available

for each traveller:
    show button("Remove", accessibleName="Remove " + uniqueTravellerLabel)
    on ordinary activation:
        remove that traveller; update checkout summary
        announce removal; move focus to next traveller control,
        otherwise previous traveller control, otherwise traveller section heading

show button("Pay", accessibleName="Pay", enabled=checkoutValid && !submitting)
on Pay activation:
    submit once; expose busy state and visible "Processing payment" status
on confirmed booking failure:
    clear busy state; preserve entered details
    show persistent failure text and backend-supported recovery action
    announce the new failure once without requiring sound
on unknown booking/payment status:
    show persistent uncertainty text and supported status-check action
    do not invite another payment until duplicate-payment risk is resolved
```

Focus destinations, single-submission handling, recovery copy and retained details are proposed interaction decisions, not verified defects or prescribed Apple APIs. Actual payment semantics and backend recovery capabilities must determine final copy and actions.

Use comfortable separated controls. Adopt 44 × 44 pt interaction areas as this design'"'s iOS target, growing with content; the supplied HIG snapshot distinguishes this default from a 28 × 28 pt minimum. No supplied dimensions establish an existing target-size failure. Standard app mode does not trigger the snapshot’s Assistive Access-specific two-confirmation rule. This audit does not mandate two confirmations for traveller removal.

## Correction and acceptance plan

Implement ranks 1–2 first to restore identifiable and operable checkout actions, then rank 3 layout changes, then ranks 4–5 status presentation. Check the combined flow after layout changes. All checks below are pending execution.

| Check | Procedure | Acceptance condition |
|---|---|---|
| Pay identity and activation | Inspect the semantic control tree; later use VoiceOver and Voice Control on a supported iPhone. Activate Pay using assistive input. | One button has the visible label and accessible name “Pay”; state changes are exposed; no duplicate icon stop; one activation produces one submission. |
| Traveller correction | Remove first, middle and last travellers with ordinary touch, VoiceOver, Switch Control and Full Keyboard Access. Include duplicate-name fixtures with distinguishable labels. | Each Remove control identifies the intended traveller, removes only that traveller, updates the summary, announces the change and leaves focus on an existing logical element. No multiple-finger gesture is required. |
| Enlargement | At the narrowest supported iPhone width, exercise every supported text size, including Larger Accessibility Text, plus a 200% enlargement fixture. Repeat with Bold Text and long content. Scroll through the full checkout. | All meaningful text remains complete, readable and operable; no clipping, overlap or obscured controls. Containers expand and crowded rows stack. At 200%, the text actually enlarges rather than merely enlarging its container. |
| Availability | Review without color; inspect and read both departure states using VoiceOver. Attempt unavailable selection. | Status text conveys availability without hue; accessible output includes time and status; selected state is distinct from availability; unavailable departure cannot enter the payable selection. |
| Failure feedback | Inject confirmed failure and unknown-status responses with audio muted; test with VoiceOver both on and off and at the largest supported text size. | A readable persistent message and valid next step appear; assistive users receive the new status once; details remain; unknown status never falsely asserts no charge or encourages unsafe repayment. |
| Complete navigation | Traverse checkout with VoiceOver, keyboard and Switch Control; exercise removal, submit, failure and recovery. Also check AssistiveTouch and Pointer Control. | Every required action is reachable and operable, traversal follows the meaningful reading sequence, focus remains visible where applicable, and dynamic updates do not strand focus. Existing order is unknown, so this is validation, not a verified violation. |
| Contrast and geometry | Obtain actual foreground/background colors, font weights, all relevant states, target bounds and spacing; measure light/dark and Increase Contrast variants. | Document measurements and fix failures against the selected criteria. Use the local snapshot’s Inspector guidance with its stated scope: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt, all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Record any separate conformance standard explicitly. Verify the chosen 44 × 44 pt control target and separation. No current contrast or size pass/fail can be assigned. |

These checks require a later runnable implementation and appropriate test equipment. On this Linux server, specification/semantic-fixture checks can be automated once implementation exists. Actual iPhone assistive-technology checks require a tester and device; Apple inspection tooling requires a suitable Mac environment. No Apple SDK is assumed here.
